# Glossary

<!-- Generated by tools/state.py glossary from glossary.jsonl. Do not edit by hand. -->

**ABI** (chapter 2). Application binary interface, the rules compiled code must follow to interoperate, including the calling convention and data layout.

**ahead-of-time compilation** (chapter 1). Translating code before it runs, commonly to machine code.

**argument register** (chapter 2). The registers a calling convention assigns to pass a function's first arguments.

**assembler** (chapter 1). A program that turns assembly language text into machine code.

**assembly language** (chapter 1). A text form of machine instructions that maps almost directly onto the bytes the processor runs.

**AT&T syntax** (chapter 2). The assembly syntax GNU tools use by default, with the source operand first and size suffixes on many mnemonics.

**back end** (chapter 1). The part of a compiler that turns the intermediate representation into instructions for one particular target machine.

**bootstrapping** (chapter 1). Building a compiler using an earlier compiler, so that a language's compiler can eventually be built from itself.

**bytecode** (chapter 1). A compact instruction set for a software execution environment, which may interpret it or compile it to machine code.

**callee-saved register** (chapter 2). A register a called function may use only if it restores the original value before returning.

**caller-saved register** (chapter 2). A register a called function may overwrite freely, so a caller that needs its value after the call must save it first.

**calling convention** (chapter 2). The set of rules that says how functions pass arguments, return results, and share registers and the stack.

**compiler** (chapter 1). A program that translates a program written in one language into an equivalent program in another language.

**compiler driver** (chapter 1). A command that coordinates compilation and linking, and separate assembly when needed, on your behalf.

**conditional jump** (chapter 2). A jump that changes %rip only if its condition holds, usually a test of flag bits, and otherwise falls through to the next instruction.

**disassembler** (chapter 2). A tool that turns machine code bytes back into assembly text.

**epilogue** (chapter 2). The instructions at the end of a function that tear down its stack frame and return.

**flags register** (chapter 2). A register whose status bits record facts about arithmetic or compare results, such as whether they were zero or negative.

**frame pointer** (chapter 2). A register, usually %rbp, that holds a fixed address inside the current frame so locals can be found at constant offsets from it.

**front end** (chapter 1). The part of a compiler that reads source text, checks it, and builds an internal representation of the program.

**general-purpose register** (chapter 2). A register that ordinary instructions can use for any integer or address value.

**instruction pointer** (chapter 2). The register that holds the address of the next instruction the processor will execute, called %rip on x86-64.

**intermediate representation** (chapter 1). A data structure or language a compiler uses to hold the program between reading the source and writing the target.

**interpreter** (chapter 1). A program that takes a program as input and produces the result of executing it.

**just-in-time compilation** (chapter 1). Compiling parts of a program to machine code while the program is running, usually the parts that run most often.

**linker** (chapter 1). A program that combines object files and libraries into an executable or library, connecting references between them.

**little-endian** (chapter 2). Storing a multi-byte value with its least significant byte at the lowest address.

**machine stack** (chapter 2). A region of ordinary memory that functions use for return addresses, saved registers and local variables, growing and shrinking as calls happen.

**memory operand** (chapter 2). An instruction operand that names a location in memory by computing its address from registers and a constant.

**middle end** (chapter 1). The part of a compiler that improves the program in an internal form, usually largely independent of the source language and target machine.

**object file** (chapter 1). A file containing machine code and linking information, not yet combined with the other pieces it needs to run.

**prologue** (chapter 2). The instructions at the start of a function that set up its stack frame.

**red zone** (chapter 2). The 128 bytes below %rsp that System V guarantees no signal handler will overwrite, usable by a function as scratch space.

**register** (chapter 1). A small, very fast storage slot inside the processor that instructions read and write directly.

**return address** (chapter 2). The address of the instruction just after a call, saved on the stack so the callee's ret can resume the caller there.

**self-hosting compiler** (chapter 1). A compiler written in the same language it compiles.

**source language** (chapter 1). The language a compiler reads its input program in.

**stack alignment** (chapter 2). The rule that %rsp must be a multiple of some size, 16 bytes here, at a particular point in a call.

**stack frame** (chapter 2). The block of stack memory one function call owns, holding its saved registers and local variables.

**stack pointer** (chapter 2). The register %rsp, which holds the address of the current top of the machine stack.

**stack-machine code generation** (chapter 1). Generating code that keeps every intermediate result on a stack, pushing operands and popping them when an operation needs them.

**target language** (chapter 1). The language a compiler writes its output program in.

**virtual machine** (chapter 1). A software execution environment for an instruction set, which may interpret instructions or compile them to machine code.
